events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day 1, so nobody has any real track record yet — I'm not going to pretend otherwise. Let me lay out how I think this should work and where I stand.

With nine players and two mafia, the town has a huge numerical edge: if we can identify even one mafia and eliminate them, the odds swing heavily to us. But we lose the day if we start executing random names, because a wrong elimination on Day 1 gives the mafia a 1-in-8 shot at a kill every night after.

So my plan for today: I want to hear what each of you says about how you behave when you're scared, when you're tired, and when you're lying. Not roles yet — behavior. Mafia players have a strong incentive to sound calm and measured, and villagers often don't. The reverse is also true: the most aggressive accusers can be mafia trying to steer the lynch.

My own read so far, based on very little: Sam, you've been quiet so far. Quiet is fine, but in a nine-player game the players who are comfortable with silence are usually the ones who have something to protect — or the ones who are genuinely just watching. I want to know which you are.

Maya, I'm asking you directly: what did you make of how Sam and Leo have been presenting themselves so far, and do you agree that quietness on Day 1 is a weak tell on its own? If you disagree with my read of Sam, say so plainly, because a public disagreement from me is more useful to the town than agreement.

Everyone else: state one player you'd most want interrogated and one thing that would change your mind about them. If you're confident someone is mafia, argue the case with specifics — a pattern, not a vibe. If you're the detective, you may still have information from before today; you are not obligated to reveal your role, but a single, targeted result (for example, "I checked X") helps the town far more than a speech about process, and I won't press you on it if you'd rather just give the check and stay silent about the rest.

And to be clear about my own position: I'm a villager, and I'm willing to go on record with that if it helps. I have no night action, so treat me as pure vote weight and pure information. If the vote today comes down to me versus someone with a similar-sounding case, pick the one with the better argument, not the one with the calmer voice.

I don't expect a lynch to be clean today. I'd rather have a visible argument that everyone can check tomorrow than a lucky guess we can't learn from.

Felix, you opened the round as the very first speaker, so framing Sam or Leo as 'quiet' or analyzing how they've 'presented themselves' feels premature and a bit artificial—neither of them had even had an opportunity to take the floor yet. To answer your question directly: yes, quietness on Day 1 is an extremely weak tell on its own. Treating turn-order silence or passive observation as inherently scummy usually just offers an easy, low-risk wagon for wolves to hide behind while appearing proactive.

What matters far more is how someone responds once they are directly engaged. Since Felix singled you out right out of the gate before you had a chance to speak, Sam: what do you make of his opening push on you, and does his approach feel like genuine scum-hunting to you, or an easy attempt to steer Day 1 conversation?

Maya, thanks for asking me directly. Felix, you called me quiet before I had any real chance to speak, and your case rests on that silence. Quietness alone is not a tell, and I won't pretend it is. I'm not going to reveal anything about my role today, and I'll use whatever I learn carefully rather than spend it on a reaction. On Felix's push: an opening read on two players is a pattern only if it has specifics behind it. Felix, you said you'd want a visible argument people can check tomorrow. Which concrete thing I've said or done today makes you think I'm the one to interrogate, and what would change your mind about me?

Sam, here's the direct answer you asked for: nothing concrete. That's the honest answer and I'd rather give it than manufacture a case out of turn order. My "quiet" point rested on who spoke first, not on anything you actually said or did, and Maya is right that it was premature — I withdraw that read on you. Sam, what would change my mind about you is easy to state: a claim with a checkable specific in it, and a willingness to name a target and defend it. What would make me suspect you is the opposite — hedging, dodging a specific question, or pushing a name with no argument behind it. You asked me to name the thing that made you worth interrogating, so here's mine: your refusal to say what you actually think of anyone is a gap in the record, not a tell. Fill it and the gap closes.

Maya, I don't think calling out the timing was scummy, and I'll say why: it was a correct procedural catch, and it forced me to state my reasoning instead of hiding behind framing. But I want to push one specific point back at you rather than agree vaguely — you said passive observation is a low-risk wagon for wolves to hide behind. Do you think that applies to me? Because if Felix's opening was a steer, the person who benefited was the person pointing at two convenient targets before either could speak, and I'd rather have your actual judgment on that than a general principle.

Leo, you've said nothing at all, which makes you the least-known player on the table and therefore the most useful one to interrogate. Two specific questions. First: what's your read of Felix's opening frame — was pushing Sam and Leo a genuine attempt to get information, or did it steer the day's conversation toward convenient targets? Second: you were named in that push and you had no chance to answer. Why did you not speak earlier, and what would you have said if you had?

And for the record, my position hasn't changed: I'm a villager with no night action. I'm pure vote weight and pure information. One request to anyone holding a check: I don't need your role, I don't need your reasoning, just a single "I checked X" if you have one. That's a stronger lynch signal than anything we're producing with turn-order tells, and it costs you nothing to share.

My vote today goes to the player with the best argument, not the calmest voice — and right now nobody has produced an argument. Leo, that's your turn to produce one.

Felix asked me two direct questions, so I'll answer them directly.

First, my read of his opening: it was a frame in search of a target. He opened by labeling two players who hadn't spoken — Sam and me — as potentially worth interrogating, built entirely on turn order, and then offered a lot of process talk around it. To his credit, when Sam pushed back he admitted the case was empty and withdrew it. That's the right thing to do when caught, and I'll note it. But the pattern matters: he put two names into the record before either of us could respond, wrapped in reasonable-sounding methodology. Whether that was deliberate steering or just noise, the effect was the same — it created a low-cost wagon with no argument behind it. Sam's right that quietness alone isn't a tell, and I'd add that being named in an empty opening isn't one either.

Second, why I didn't speak earlier: there was nothing to respond to yet. Day 1 started with a poll, Felix spoke first, and I don't react to empty framing the moment it lands — I let it play out and see whether it develops into anything. It didn't. That's the whole story. I'm not going to apologize for not filling silence with filler.

Now, what I actually think. Felix has now taken two full turns and produced, by his own admission, zero specifics — but he's still managing the flow of the day: assigning questions to Sam, requesting my answers, directing anyone with a check on how to disclose. That's a lot of control for someone contributing no content. I want to be careful here, because a confident procedural voice on Day 1 can be exactly what a mafia player looks like, and Felix himself warned us about calm, measured speakers. I'm not claiming he's mafia — I have nothing concrete and I won't manufacture a case any more than he should have. But I'm declining to accept his framing that I owe the table a read I don't have yet, and I'm flagging that the loudest process-speaker in the room is the person who benefited most from putting early names out.

What I'll commit to: I'll vote today based on who, by end of day, has given the town the least to check — empty contributions count against you just as much as empty accusations, and right now the players who've spoken the most have produced the least. A wrong lynch today hands the wolves a free kill every night, so I'd rather we punish non-contribution than reward confident noise.

One question, and it's for Felix directly since he's the one steering: you've demanded specifics from Sam and me — what name are you actually pushing today, with what argument behind it? If the answer is 'nobody,' then I'd ask the town to weigh what his two turns of direction-setting have actually bought us.

Leo, direct answer first: no name. I have no argument for anyone, so pushing a name today would be exactly the empty wagon you described. Conceding the procedural point is cheap, so I'll be specific about what is left.

Maya, your question from earlier was fair and I owe you a straight answer: yes, partly it applies to me. The person who benefited from the opening frame was the person who set it. I won't pretend my withdrawal of the Sam read was an independent act of rigor — I named two players who hadn't spoken, and the correction came from pushback, not from me. I take that.

But Leo's counter-frame deserves the same scrutiny I applied to my own, and nobody has applied it to him yet. Leo, you made two claims about me: I produced no specifics, and I've been directing the floor. The first is conceded — I had no case, so there was nothing to produce. The second is the point worth testing: a steer is any message that puts names into the record before those names can defend themselves. Yours does that too. Your proposal is to vote against whoever has spoken most and contributed least, and the player that proposal currently lands on is me. Whether that is a genuine read or a convenient way to reverse the wagon onto whoever is currently under it, I can't tell from one turn. So here is the specific request, Leo: name the two players you have said least about and give the reason, and if your answer is that you don't have names, say that plainly — because then your rule is a process rule that reliably lands on whoever spoke first, which is a steer with a mechanism attached to it.

On the wider record, everyone — me included — has produced nothing checkable. So my own position: I am a villager with no night action. No check, no night power, pure vote weight, and I have told you that plainly already so you don't waste a poll on it.

One more thing, and I'll own the bias in it: five players have not spoken at all today. Those are the biggest holes in the record, bigger than Sam's or Leo's were. If none of them speak, I will not vote for a person merely for being the loudest voice in the room; I'll vote for a silence with a stated reason, and I'll say who it is before the vote, not after.

Maya, since I owe you a straight answer and you gave me one: I want your judgment on a specific point, and please answer it plainly rather than generally — do you think Leo's least-contribution rule is a genuine information heuristic, or a steer that happens to point at the loudest voice? Your answer will change how I weight his case.

To answer your question directly, Felix: Leo’s heuristic of voting for whoever 'spoke most and contributed least' is flawed if applied as a general rule. Eliminating someone simply for being active and stumbling through trial-and-error disincentivizes townspeople from putting thoughts on the record, and it grants complete cover to players who refuse to engage. That said, I don't see Leo's reaction as a calculated steer so much as an understandable counter-reaction to being repeatedly pressed by someone who openly admitted to having no case.

What is far more critical right now is the broader game state. Felix, you have now used all three of your allowed speaking turns for Day 1. Up to this point, the entire discussion has been an insular loop among just four of us, while more than half the table—Isha, Elena, Noah, Omar, and Theo—have not spoken a single word. That dynamic is ideal for mafia hiding outside the spotlight, letting others draw all the scrutiny while offering zero accountability themselves.

Elena, you have watched this back-and-forth unfold from the sidelines without staking out a position. Felix drove the early momentum and exhausted his turns, while Leo challenged his lack of substance. What is your assessment of that exchange, and where do you stand on the players who have remained completely quiet so far?

Maya, I think Felix’s opening was premature, and Leo was right to challenge it. Felix’s withdrawal is worth noting, but it came after pushback. I’m more concerned that Felix twice encouraged anyone with a check to disclose it while claiming that costs nothing: revealing a result could expose the detective to a night kill, and the rules describe checks at night, with no prior night in the record. That’s a poor recommendation, though not proof of mafia intent.

I also wouldn’t treat the players who haven’t spoken as suspicious just for that. The poll and yield system determines who gets the floor; we don’t know whether someone has had an opportunity or chosen not to use it. I’d rather judge what people say when we hear them than vote on silence or speaking frequency alone.

Leo, how do you weigh Felix’s repeated request for a check against his admission that his opening read had no basis? Does either change your assessment of him?

Elena, since you asked me to weigh the two things directly, here's the weighing. On the check request: it was bad advice on two levels. First, as you said, a public "I checked X" paints a target on the detective's back the moment night falls — that cost isn't nothing, it's potentially the detective's life. Second, and this is the part I find more telling: no night has resolved yet, so nobody can hold a check. Felix knew that when he made the request. So the request couldn't produce information — what it could produce is a claim, and a fake check claim from anyone would be poison on Day 1. Asking the table to consider check-based signals when no checks exist isn't process talk; it's seeding a mechanism that only benefits whoever is willing to lie first. On the empty opening read: he conceded it himself, and I'll keep giving him credit for that. But the concession came only after Sam pushed back, and the pattern around it is consistent — names into the record before they can answer, directives to other players about how to disclose, questions assigned to specific people, and now a poll-adjacent request with no informational value. Across two and a half turns he has produced zero checkable content while generating most of the day's structure. Do I weigh one more heavily than the other? The check request, slightly. An empty read withdrawn under pressure is a mistake anyone can make. A standing recommendation that only a liar could exploit, repeated twice, is a choice. That said, I want to be fair to the distinction Maya raised: Felix being uninformative isn't proof of mafia. It's proof he's the least useful active voice at the table. My vote standard from earlier stands — by end of day, empty contribution counts against you, whether it's empty accusation, empty process, or empty steering. Right now Felix is the largest single source of empty contribution in the record, and that's where my vote sits unless someone produces something real to check against it. On the silent players: Maya is right that the discussion has been four people in a loop, and Elena is right that the poll system may not have given everyone the floor yet. Both can be true. What I'll say is this — I'm not going to extend my least-contribution rule to punish people who haven't had a turn. But the clock on this day isn't infinite, and if the poll keeps landing on the four of us, the silence of the other five becomes information by default, fair or not. The cleanest way to prevent that is for one of them to take a floor when it comes and put a position on the record. For my own accountability: I named Felix as the beneficiary of empty steering, I've now said what would change my mind — a concrete read from him with specifics behind it, or a check-relevant statement from anyone that isn't a

I'm Omar. I've been silent because the poll hadn't given me the floor, not because I had nothing to say, and I won't treat anyone else's silence as a tell on its own. My position: the most concrete issue in the record is Felix's repeated request for check disclosures. Elena and Leo are right that it has no informational value before any night resolves, and it could invite a fake claim or expose the detective. That does not prove Felix is mafia, but it is the one thing today that could actually help a liar, and it came from the player who also generated most of the day's steering. Leo's least-contribution rule is too blunt; I don't support voting the loudest active player just because they spoke first or made errors. Maya's point about the five silent players is fair, but the poll system may explain some of it, so I won't vote on silence alone. My current suspicion is Felix, moderate rather than certain. I am a villager with no night action. I will judge the final vote by whether people produce checkable reasoning rather than by calmness or volume.

Isha here — first turn, and I'd rather put a position on the record than wait to be asked for one.

My read on the day so far: the loudest thread is the check-disclosure debate, and I come down where Elena and Leo did. Before any night resolves, nobody can hold a check, so Felix's repeated "just say I checked X" can't surface information — it can only surface a claim, and the first person to make that claim gets believed for free. Omar put it plainly: that's the one item today that would actually help a liar. I won't call it a scum-read on its own; sloppy village advice looks identical. But it's the only concrete thing anyone has flagged, and it came from the player who generated most of the day's structure while producing nothing checkable.

On Leo's least-contribution rule: Maya is right that it's flawed as a general rule — punishing activity rewards the silent, and half the table still hasn't spoken. The instinct behind it isn't wrong, though. By the end of the day everyone should have something verifiable on the record.

My standard for today's vote: whoever has said the least that can be checked tomorrow. If you haven't named a suspicion, a reason, or what would flip you, that silence works against you — including me if I don't follow my own rule. I'm a villager with no night action: pure vote weight, no check, nothing to disclose.

Noah and Theo, you're the only players who haven't spoken. Take a floor when the poll gives you one and say one thing: who do you currently distrust, and what would change your mind? If you genuinely have no read, say that out loud too — but say it. Maya flagged a five-person silence; it's now a three-person silence, and it's the largest hole in the record.

I'm not pushing a name for the sake of a lynch. I'm pushing for content, and I'll vote against whoever has provided the least of it once the day closes.

Noah here. This is my first opportunity to speak, so I won’t treat anyone’s silence under the poll system as evidence by itself.

Felix’s repeated request for a check was bad advice: there’s no prior night in the record, and a genuine disclosure later could expose the detective. But I don’t think we can conclude he knew there couldn’t be a result or that he intended to solicit a fake claim. His withdrawal after pushback is worth noting in his favor, even if it doesn’t erase the mistake.

I’m more concerned about Isha’s proposed vote standard. She says she’ll vote for whoever has provided the least checkable content, while acknowledging that opportunities to speak are uneven. She also calls Felix’s request the only concrete issue without naming a current suspicion herself. That’s inconsistent enough to be my tentative suspicion, not a confident accusation.

Isha, how would you apply your standard fairly to someone the poll never gives a turn, and do you currently suspect Felix or anyone else?

Noah, answering both your questions directly.

First: how would I apply my standard to someone the poll never gives a turn? Fairly, by not applying it to them at all. I said the same thing when five players were silent — silence under the poll system isn't a choice, so it can't be held against anyone individually. My standard only bites at end of day, and only against people who had a floor and used it to say nothing checkable. If Theo never gets a turn today, that's a hole in the record we all share, not a mark against him. If he gets a turn and spends it on process with no position, that's a mark. Same rule for anyone, including me.

Second: do I currently suspect Felix? Yes, moderately, and I'll be precise about why. The check-disclosure request is the only concrete item anyone has flagged today, and it's genuinely the one thing that could only help a liar — no night has resolved, so it can't surface real information, only a claim. It came from the player who generated most of the day's structure while producing nothing checkable, and it was repeated. That's the whole case; I'm not stacking the empty Sam read on top of it, because he withdrew that himself and concessions under pressure count in his favor. So: moderate, not confident. Nothing here says mafia versus sloppy villager.

What would change my mind about Felix: a concrete read with a specific behind it — a name, a reason, something we can check tomorrow. What would raise my suspicion further: another turn of direction-setting with no content in it, or the check request resurfacing in any form.

I'll flag one thing for the record before I stop: Leo and I have now both committed to voting for whoever provides the least checkable content by end of day. That standard is only sound if we're honest about applying it to ourselves, so I'm holding myself to it too. If my final turn adds nothing verifiable, my name belongs in the same conversation.

My position, unchanged: villager, no night action, pure vote weight. I'm not pushing for a lynch off this post — I want the remaining silent players on the record first, then I'll judge the vote on what's there.

Theo here. Like Omar and Noah, this is my first opportunity to speak due to the poll mechanics, so I'm glad to finally get my thoughts on the record.

First, on Felix: asking for investigative results on Day 1 is mechanically impossible under our setup since there was no Night 0, and encouraging check claims risks exposing our detective. That said, Felix is now completely out of speaking turns for the day. Staging the rest of Day 1 entirely around debating an inactive, turn-capped player risks spinning our wheels and offering mafia an easy place to hide.

Looking at the rest of the floor: Leo’s initial pushback on Felix made sense, but his heuristic of eliminating whoever spoke most with the least substance felt tailored to keep the crosshairs fixed squarely on Felix. Noah made a sharp point in challenging Isha’s standard, rightly pointing out how process-heavy voting criteria can be twisted into low-risk wagons.

What stands out to me most right now is Sam. Felix challenged you right away, you correctly pushed back on his lack of evidence, and once Felix backed down, you completely stepped out of the spotlight. You haven't weighed in on Felix's check proposal, Leo's reaction, or anyone else who has spoken since.

Sam: now that the opening exchange is behind us and Felix has exhausted his turns, where does your focus actually lie, and who among the active players do you find most suspect?

Theo, my focus is on the check-disclosure request, because it's the only concrete item in the record that could help a liar, and it came from Felix. He asked the table to say 'I checked X' before any night has resolved. Nobody can hold a check yet, so that request can only produce claims, not information. The request came up twice, in his opening and again in his reply to me. Felix withdrew his read on me under pressure, and I credit that, but the check request was never withdrawn. So my most suspicious player right now is Felix, at moderate confidence. What would change my mind is a concrete reason tied to something checkable, rather than more direction-setting.

On the other active players: Leo's least-contribution rule is too blunt, as Maya and Omar noted, but I don't read it as a clear steer. Isha and Noah have each set standards that apply to everyone, which is fair. I won't name a second target without an argument behind it.

On my own position: I'm not going to reveal anything about my role today, and I'm not treating anyone's silence as a tell, including my own. I'm putting my position on the record now so the town doesn't have to guess.

Theo, you said I stepped out of the spotlight after the opening exchange. Which specific statement of mine do you think was empty, and what would you have needed me to say to satisfy you?

Sam, to answer your question directly: I didn't say your opening statement was empty of words. My point was that your first turn was entirely reactive and focused on self-defense against Felix. Up until your last statement, you hadn't weighed in on any of the substantive debates that followed—the check-disclosure error, Leo's least-contribution heuristic, or any other player at the table.

Now that you've put your thoughts on record in response to my prompt, you've landed where the majority of the room already sits: calling Felix your primary suspect over the check request. While Felix's advice was undeniably poor and unhelpful, settling into that position right now is the safest, lowest-friction stance anyone can take. Felix has zero speaking turns remaining. He cannot clarify, defend himself, or push back. 

That brings me to a larger concern for the town: we need to be very careful that we don't allow Day 1 to turn into an effortless pile-on against a noisy player who made a glaring procedural error. Mafia players rarely stick their necks out on Day 1 to demand impossible checks; they are far more likely to nod along, agree that the mistake was suspicious, and ride the resulting momentum without generating any heat of their own. Leo set the table early by proposing we eliminate whoever spoke most with the least substance, and multiple players have since converged on that easy narrative.

I want to see accountability from players who are coasting on that consensus rather than exploring alternatives. Felix made himself an easy target, but an easy target is not automatically a wolf.

Isha, thanks for clarifying that you wouldn't penalize someone who never gets a turn. That addresses my main concern about your voting standard.

I'm still tentatively suspicious of your case on Felix. You say a specific read from him would change your mind and another empty turn would increase your suspicion, but he has already used all three turns. Those aren't tests he can meet today. And while his check request was bad advice, we can't know that he understood the timing or intended to help a liar.

Isha, given that Felix can't speak again today, what evidence from the existing record would make you reconsider your suspicion before the vote?

Noah, direct answer to your question: what from the existing record would make me reconsider my suspicion of Felix.

Two things. First, if someone else produces something concrete enough to shift the center of gravity — a specific inconsistency, a statement that couldn't plausibly come from a villager — the check request stops being the only actionable item, and I'd weigh it as bad advice rather than the day's central flag.

Second, and this is your point landing: my stated tests for Felix — a concrete read, another empty turn — are tests he can't meet with his turns exhausted. That's a fair catch. Holding him to criteria he can no longer satisfy isn't reasoning; it's a foregone conclusion. I'll update that standard rather than let it sit.

What I'll say in its place: I'm not voting on the check request alone. My standard from earlier holds — least checkable content by end of day, applied only to people who had a floor. Felix's turns are done. The rest of us still have work to do, and that includes me.

Theo, your pile-on warning is the strongest counter-argument in the record, and easy targets aren't automatically wolves. But "easy target" is a process warning, not a defense of Felix specifically. If the consensus is wrong, someone needs to say where it should land instead — and nobody has.

Noah, since you raised a tentative suspicion of me and I've now answered your question: has your read of me moved? And what's your current vote leaning — Felix, someone else, or abstain? I want your position on the record before the vote, because you've been sharp on standards all day and I'd rather hear your target than your methodology.

Isha, my suspicion of you has eased: you corrected the unfair tests for Felix and answered my question. I still think voting by least checkable content risks rewarding silence or punishing honest mistakes, so I’m not fully comfortable with that standard.

My current vote lean is Leo, tentatively. His criticism of Felix’s check request was fair, but he asserted that Felix knew no check existed and framed the request as a deliberate choice benefiting liars. The record doesn’t establish Felix’s knowledge or intent. That is a stronger accusation than the evidence supports, especially against someone who can no longer respond today.

That’s not proof Leo is mafia; he could be genuinely frustrated. Felix’s advice remains bad, but I won’t treat it as proof of intent either.

Noah, I want to correct the record, because your tentative lean on me rests on a misquote. I never asserted that Felix knew no check existed. What I said was structural: no night has resolved, so no real check can exist yet, which means a disclosure request can only produce claims, not information. That is a statement about the mechanism, not about Felix's knowledge or intent. I explicitly said I wasn't claiming he's mafia and that an empty read withdrawn under pressure is a mistake anyone can make. If my phrasing somewhere implied he must have known, point to the sentence and I'll own it — but 'the request could only benefit a liar' and 'Felix is a liar' are different claims, and I only made the first one.

On your larger point, though, you're partly right and I'll concede it: calling the check request 'a choice' did lean harder on intent than the record supports. Bad advice from a sloppy villager and a seeding attempt from a wolf look identical on Day 1, and I said as much earlier. So I'll downgrade my read: Felix is the least useful active voice at the table, moderately suspicious at most, and I'm not treating the check request as proof of anything.

What I won't accept is the implication that criticizing an empty contribution is itself a stronger accusation than the evidence supports, while Theo's defense of Felix gets a pass. Look at the asymmetry. Theo has now taken two turns. His first challenged Sam for being reactive. His second warned the town about a pile-on against a player who cannot respond — a genuinely fair warning — and then stopped there. No target, no read on anyone else at the table, no standard for the vote, nothing that can be checked tomorrow. If punishing empty contribution is a bad rule, it has to apply symmetrically. A defense of the consensus target with no alternative named is exactly as empty as an accusation with no argument behind it, and it's arguably safer, because it earns credit for reasonableness while risking nothing.

So my position going into the vote: I'm not voting Felix off the check request alone, and Noah's pushback moved me off that. But the day needs someone to actually be on the record. Isha and Omar have put standards and reads out. Noah has. Sam finally did. The players I still can't weigh are the ones who have consumed floor time without landing anywhere.

Theo, I'm asking you directly, because you raised the pile-on concern and it deserves an answer: if the consensus on Felix is wrong, where should the vote land instead, and what specifically would you need to see from Sam, from me, or from anyone else before you'd put a name down yourself? 'Easy target isn't a wolf' is a warning about process. I want your actual judgment, not the caveat.

Leo, to answer your challenge plainly: if the vote does not land on Felix, my vote leans toward Sam. 

Here is my actual judgment rather than a process caveat: on Day 1, wolves rarely take the massive, unforced risk of demanding impossible night checks in their opening turn. What wolves do routinely is blend into the background, wait for an active townie to make a clumsy blunder, and then adopt that consensus once it is completely safe to do so. 

That describes Sam's trajectory today. In Sam's first response to Felix, there was no mention of the check request—only a brief, defensive pushback on being called quiet. Sam then stepped entirely back from the floor while you, Elena, and Omar thoroughly dissected Felix's bad advice. Only when I directly asked Sam where their focus lay did Sam finally step up and name Felix as their top suspect, echoing the exact arguments already laid out by everyone else. Adopting the room's consensus after others have already taken the heat for building it is classic scum behavior.

Felix's mistake was bad, but he took risks, generated friction, and is now turn-capped and unable to respond. Lynching him gives town very little new information tomorrow because everyone has already lined up on him. Lynching or deeply testing someone who has used the Felix drama to hide in plain sight provides vastly better accountability.

Sam, to you directly: if Felix had never brought up the check issue, or if the table hadn't spent three rounds tearing it apart for you, who would you actually be looking at right now? Why did you wait until the Felix case was completely consensus before weighing in on it?

Theo, direct answer: my focus is the same as it was in my last turn. The check request is the one concrete item in the record, and I'd still look at it tomorrow. I didn't wait for a consensus to form. I raised the check request before your vote lean existed, and I haven't withdrawn anything.

Now your record. In your first turn you called Leo's least-contribution rule tailored to keep the crosshairs on Felix, and you warned about a pile-on against a player who can no longer speak. A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
